\begin{abstract}
We study a drone delivery routing problem in which energy consumption depends on
both distance and carried payload, under battery, payload, fleet-size and no-fly
constraints. We give two distinct mathematical formulations, prove NP-hardness by
reduction from TSP, and implement five methods on a shared objective: a greedy
construction, an exact Branch \& Bound with an anytime dual bound, a Genetic
Algorithm, Simulated Annealing, and Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search. No-fly
zones are modelled geometrically as polygons, with legs detoured around them
along visibility-graph shortest paths rather than deleted. On the instances
Branch \& Bound solves to proven optimality every metaheuristic reaches the
optimum; beyond that size the exact method times out and the metaheuristics
dominate, with ALNS strongest. This is the expected crossover between exact and
approximate methods, and we quantify where it occurs.
\end{abstract}

\tableofcontents

% ===========================================================================
\section{Problem Definition}

A logistics company operates a homogeneous fleet of $K$ drones based at a central
depot (node $0$). Each of $n$ customers must be served exactly once. Each drone
flies a single route depot $\rightarrow$ customers $\rightarrow$ depot. We
\emph{minimise total energy} subject to: each customer served once; routes
start and end at the depot; per-drone battery $B$ and payload $Q$ limits; route
connectivity; and forbidden no-fly arcs $F$.

\paragraph{Notation.}
$V=\{0,\dots,n\}$, customers $V_c=\{1,\dots,n\}$, demands $q_i>0$ with $q_0=0$,
and Euclidean distances $d_{ij}$.

\subsection{Energy model}

Energy scales with distance \emph{and} with onboard carried weight. Traversing
arc $(i,j)$ carrying weight $w$ costs
\[
  e_{ij}(w) = d_{ij}\,(\alpha + \beta\,w),
\]
with $\alpha>0$ (the drone's own mass per unit distance) and $\beta\ge 0$ (energy
per unit distance per unit carried weight). A drone loads its route's total demand
at the depot and sheds weight at each delivery, so onboard weight \emph{decreases}
along the route. This makes energy \textbf{route-order dependent}, which is what
separates the problem from a plain distance-based VRP: two routes visiting the
same customers in different orders have different costs.

The linear-in-payload model follows the multirotor drone literature
(Dorling et al., \emph{IEEE Trans.\ Transp.\ Electrif.}\ 3(4), 2017). Experiments
use $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0.3$, i.e.\ a fully loaded drone consumes roughly
$30\%$ more energy per unit distance than an empty one, consistent with published
measurements for small commercial multirotors. Coordinates are normalised to a
$100$-unit grid, which makes these values dimensionally convenient while
preserving relative structure.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Two Mathematical Formulations}

\subsection{Formulation 1 --- Arc-based MILP}

Binary arc variables $x_{ij}$, flow (onboard weight) variables $f_{ij}$, and
energy potentials $u_i$:
\[
  \min \sum_{(i,j)} d_{ij}\,(\alpha x_{ij} + \beta f_{ij})
\]
subject to in/out degree $1$ at each customer,
\[
  \sum_{j} x_{0j} \le K,
  \qquad
  \sum_j f_{ij}-\sum_j f_{ji} = -q_i \quad \forall i \in V_c,
  \qquad
  f_{ij}\le Q\,x_{ij},
\]
\[
  u_j \ge u_i + e_{ij}(f_{ij}) - M(1-x_{ij}),
  \qquad
  u_i \le B,
  \qquad
  x_{ij}=0 \;\; \forall (i,j)\in F .
\]
The flow variables do double duty: they linearise the load-dependent energy term
and they eliminate subtours, since a disconnected cycle cannot satisfy weight
conservation.

\subsection{Formulation 2 --- Commodity-flow model}

A single commodity of ``undelivered packages'': the depot emits $\sum_i q_i$ and
each customer $i$ absorbs $q_i$. Variables are the commodity flow $g_{ij}\ge 0$
and integer traversal counts $y_{ij}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$:
\[
  \min \sum_{(i,j)} d_{ij}\,(\alpha y_{ij} + \beta g_{ij})
\]
subject to commodity conservation, capacity $g_{ij}\le Q\,y_{ij}$, drone
continuity $\sum_j y_{ij}=\sum_j y_{ji}$, and the fleet cap
$\sum_j y_{0j}\le K$.

\paragraph{These are genuinely different models, not reformulations.}
Formulation 1 \emph{sequences} nodes using an ordering potential $(x,u)$;
Formulation 2 \emph{conserves commodity} with traversal counts $(g,y)$ and has no
ordering variable at all. Formulation 2 is implemented and solved with CBC in the
notebook (section 6b). Because it expresses the battery limit as a path
constraint that it does not carry, it yields a valid \emph{lower bound}: it agrees
exactly with the Branch \& Bound optimum on instances where the battery does not
bind, and falls below it when the battery is active. The notebook verifies this
relationship on every instance with $n \le 8$.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Complexity Analysis}

\begin{theorem}
The problem is NP-hard, even with one drone, $\beta=0$, no no-fly zones, and
infinite payload and battery.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Reduction from TSP. Given a TSP instance on cities $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with distances
$d_{ij}$, build an instance with the same customers, $K=1$, $\beta=0$ (so
$e_{ij}=\alpha d_{ij}$), $Q=B=\infty$ and $F=\varnothing$. A feasible solution is
then exactly one closed tour through all customers from the depot, with energy
$\alpha\sum d_{ij}$. The minimum-energy solution is therefore a minimum-length
Hamiltonian tour, i.e.\ an optimal TSP tour. The reduction is polynomial, so the
problem is NP-hard.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Feasibility is NP-complete.}
Deciding whether the customers can be partitioned into $\le K$ groups of total
demand $\le Q$ is exactly Bin Packing, and a candidate fleet assignment is
checkable in polynomial time.

\paragraph{Consequence.}
The number of partitions-into-ordered-routes grows faster than $n!$, so explicit
enumeration is impractical. This motivates Branch \& Bound for small $n$ and
metaheuristics for larger $n$ --- precisely the trade-off measured in section~\ref{sec:results}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Instance Generation}

Instances are generated reproducibly from a seed. Customers are placed uniformly
at random in a $100\times100$ square with the depot at the centre; demands are
drawn uniformly from $[1,5]$.

Payload is sized as a slack multiple of the minimum feasible per-drone capacity,
$Q = 1.7 \cdot (\sum_i q_i)/K$, so that the fleet can carry all demand but a
drone can take several customers rather than exactly its share --- this keeps the
partitioning decision non-trivial. The battery is calibrated against a
nearest-neighbour tour cost divided across the fleet, so feasible partitions exist
but loose routes genuinely risk exceeding the limit rather than the constraint
being vacuous.

\subsection{No-fly zones: forbidden edges versus polygonal detours}

Two representations are implemented, and the difference is substantive.

The first models a zone as a set of forbidden \emph{edges}: a fraction of the
longest customer-to-customer edges, mimicking restricted air corridors between
distant nodes. Depot edges are never forbidden, so a feasible solution always
exists. This is a convenient proxy, but it is not what a no-fly zone is: it
deletes the connection entirely, as though a customer behind a restricted area
became unreachable.

The second is geometric and is the one we prefer. A zone is a \emph{polygon}, and
a leg that would cross one is not deleted but \emph{detoured}: the drone flies
the shortest obstacle-avoiding path around it. That path is computed on a
visibility graph whose nodes are the depot, the customers and every polygon
vertex, with an edge between two nodes exactly when the segment joining them does
not enter a zone's interior; a shortest path in that graph is an optimal path in
the polygonal domain, since such a path turns only at obstacle vertices.

The resulting detour lengths are folded into the distance matrix, which is
computed once per instance and cached. The crucial consequence is that
\textbf{no solver changes at all}: Branch \& Bound, the GA, SA and ALNS keep
working unmodified and simply see a cost structure that reflects real geography.
The detours also make the cost matrix structured rather than randomly punched
full of holes, which is a more faithful model of restricted airspace.

The benchmark suite has 12 instances from $n=5$ to $n=30$, spanning the range
where Branch \& Bound is tractable through to where only the metaheuristics
remain useful. Four of them carry no-fly zones.

\section{Solution Methods}

All four methods share one implementation of the objective and the feasibility
check, so the comparison is fair by construction.

\subsection{Constructive heuristics}

Two constructions provide warm starts: a nearest-neighbour builder that opens a
new drone when payload, battery or a no-fly edge blocks extension, and a
Clarke--Wright savings construction adapted to the energy objective, which merges
route endpoints in decreasing order of savings while feasibility holds. The
cheaper of the two is used.

\subsection{Exact method --- Branch \& Bound}

Depth-first implicit enumeration over partitions into ordered routes.

\paragraph{Branching.} At each node we either (A) append an unassigned customer
to the currently open route, or (B) close the open route and start a new one,
consuming a drone. Successive routes are forced to start with strictly increasing
first-customer indices, a symmetry break that generates each
partition-into-ordered-routes exactly once.

\paragraph{Lower bound.} For a partial solution with committed energy $c$ and
unassigned set $U$,
\[
  \mathrm{LB} = c + \sum_{v \in U} \alpha \cdot \min_{j \ne v,\,(j,v)\notin F} d_{jv}.
\]
Every unassigned customer must be entered by at least one edge in any completion;
$\alpha$ is the minimum per-distance coefficient and $\beta w \ge 0$, so the sum
never overestimates the remaining cost. The bound is the routing analogue of the
assignment-problem column-minimum bound.

\paragraph{Pruning.} A node is discarded (becomes a sterile set) when
$\mathrm{LB} \ge$ incumbent, and also on any payload, battery or no-fly violation.
A wall-clock limit is applied; if the tree is exhausted within it, the returned
solution is \emph{provably optimal}, and the implementation reports this
explicitly.

\paragraph{Anytime dual bound.}
A depth-first search stopped by its clock used to report only its incumbent,
which -- warm-started from greedy -- was frequently \emph{still the greedy
value}, with nothing to say about how far from optimal it was. We now also
report a valid global lower bound, so every run brackets the optimum:
\[
  \mathrm{dual\ bound} \;\le\; \mathrm{optimum} \;\le\; \mathrm{incumbent}.
\]
The construction needs care. It is not sufficient to record the bound of the node
occupied when time expired: the unexplored space also contains every sibling not
yet reached, and those may be cheaper. Each frame therefore materialises its
children together with their bounds before descending, and on unwinding
contributes the bounds of the children it never entered. Nodes pruned as sterile
contribute nothing, correctly, since their bound already exceeds the incumbent.
The minimum over that frontier is a true lower bound on the optimum; when the
tree is exhausted it meets the incumbent and optimality is proved.

The bound itself remains weak -- the column-minimum bound is precisely why the
search stalls near $n=9$ -- so the reported gaps on large instances are wide.
Strengthening it (Held--Karp 1-trees with subgradient ascent, the LP relaxation
of Formulation~1, or set-partitioning with column generation) is the natural next
step, and would push proven optimality substantially past $n=9$.

\subsection{Encoding: giant tour + optimal Split}
\label{sec:split}

Both metaheuristics share one problem-specific encoding. A chromosome is a
\emph{giant tour}: a permutation of all customers with no route delimiters. A
dynamic-programming \textbf{Split} then cuts it into the energy-optimal set of
$\le K$ feasible routes.

Node $i$ of the auxiliary graph means ``the first $i$ customers of the giant tour
have been covered''. Arc $(i \rightarrow j)$ is a single drone route serving
positions $i+1,\dots,j$ in that order, weighted by that route's energy, or
$\infty$ if the segment violates payload, battery or a no-fly edge. Any path
$0 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow n$ is therefore a partition of the tour into
consecutive routes whose total arc weight is the fleet energy, and the shortest
such path is the optimal segmentation \emph{for that ordering}. The DP carries a
second index, giving states $(i,k)$ = ``first $i$ customers covered using exactly
$k$ routes''; the answer is $\min_{k \le K} \mathrm{dp}[n][k]$, so the fleet
constraint is enforced exactly rather than by penalty.

This is the key design decision of the implementation: crossover and mutation act
on permutations and are therefore always valid, and \emph{all} feasibility
handling lives inside Split.

\subsection{Genetic Algorithm}

Population-based search over giant tours. Binary tournament selection; Order
Crossover (OX), which preserves relative order and is the natural recombination
for permutations; swap mutation and 2-opt segment-reversal mutation; and elitism
so the best individuals always survive. Fitness is the Split-decoded energy; a
chromosome that Split cannot fit into $K$ drones receives an infinite cost and
dies out. The population is seeded with the greedy warm start plus random
permutations.

\subsection{Simulated Annealing}

Local search over the same encoding, so the two metaheuristics are directly
comparable. SA extends plain descent by accepting a worsening move of size
$\Delta$ with probability $\exp(-\Delta/T)$, which lets it escape the local optima
that trap hill-climbing. The neighbourhood is compound --- 2-opt reversal, swap,
and or-move (relocate one customer) --- drawn at random each iteration. Cooling is
geometric, $T \leftarrow \gamma T$ with $\gamma = 0.9995$, and the initial
temperature is calibrated from the average move delta so that early acceptance is
about $0.8$. On stagnation the search reheats to $T_0/2$ and restarts from the
incumbent, adding diversification.

\subsection{Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search}

Where Simulated Annealing perturbs a tour by a single move, ALNS repeatedly
\emph{destroys} a substantial part of the solution and \emph{repairs} it, moving
through the search space in far larger and better-directed steps.

\paragraph{Destroy operators.} Random removal (diversification); worst removal,
dropping the customers contributing the largest detour; Shaw removal, dropping a
seed customer together with its nearest relatives so the repair can re-group a
whole neighbourhood; and route removal, emptying one drone entirely and forcing
its customers to be redistributed.

\paragraph{Repair operators.} Greedy insertion, placing each customer in its
cheapest position; and regret-2 and regret-3 insertion, which instead insert the
customer that would suffer most from waiting, measured as the gap between its
best and $k$-th best position. That look-ahead is what plain greedy lacks.

\paragraph{Scoring insertions by energy, not distance.}
The obvious insertion cost is the distance detour
$d_{pc}+d_{cn}-d_{pn}$, and it is wrong here. Because a drone loads its whole
route at the depot and sheds weight at each delivery, placing customer $c$ later
in a route means hauling its parcel $q_c$ across every leg before it --- exactly
the order-dependence that defines this problem. Scoring by detour alone ignores
that, and in our first implementation the search converged efficiently to
solutions that were short but not cheap, missing proven optima that the GA and SA
both found. The cost therefore charges
\[
  \alpha\,(d_{pc}+d_{cn}-d_{pn}) \;+\; \beta\, q_c \, D(\text{pos}),
\]
where $D(\text{pos})$ is the distance already flown before the insertion point.
With that correction ALNS recovers every proven optimum.

\paragraph{Randomised repair.}
Greedy and regret insertion are deterministic given the remaining tour, so
destroy-and-repair regenerates the same few solutions and the search stalls: we
measured 400 rounds producing only four distinct tours on an eight-customer
instance. Each candidate position is therefore perturbed by
$\eta \cdot d_{\max} \cdot U(-1,1)$, the standard ALNS noise term.

\paragraph{Adaptivity.} Each operator carries a weight, updated after every
segment of iterations from the scores it earned -- a large reward for a new
global best, less for an improving or merely accepted move -- so operators that
are working get selected more often. Acceptance is annealing-style, so the search
can still escape local optima. Feasibility is delegated to Split exactly as in
the GA and SA, so all three search the same space and are directly comparable.

\section{Comparative Analysis}

\subsection{Reading the crossover correctly}

On the larger instances the Branch \& Bound column is \emph{worse} (higher energy)
than GA and SA. Since Branch \& Bound is the exact method, this looks
contradictory. It is not, and the interpretation matters:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Branch \& Bound is exact only if it runs to completion.} The problem
is NP-hard and the search tree grows roughly exponentially, so we impose a
wall-clock limit.

\item \textbf{On the small instances} the tree is exhausted within the limit, so
the method returns a \emph{proven optimum}. There, GA and SA match it exactly, at
a $0\%$ gap. This is strong evidence that all three implementations are correct:
a heuristic can never beat a true optimum, and neither does.

\item \textbf{On the larger instances} the tree is far too big to finish, so
Branch \& Bound is cut off early and returns only its incumbent. Because it was
warm-started from the greedy construction, that incumbent is often \emph{still the
greedy value} --- which is exactly why the Branch \& Bound bar equals the greedy
bar on the large instances in the comparison figure.
\end{itemize}

The metaheuristics, meanwhile, keep improving for their whole time budget and pull
ahead. \textbf{They are not beating the true optimum --- they are beating Branch \&
Bound's incomplete, timed-out answer.} Given astronomically longer, the exact
method would eventually match or beat them.

So the experiment shows the expected and correct story: exact methods win, with a
proof, while they remain tractable; metaheuristics take over once exactness
becomes too expensive. That crossover is the entire motivation for studying
metaheuristics, and these results locate it empirically.

\subsection{Comparing the three metaheuristics}

All three reach the optimum on the instances where one is known, which is the
correctness check; they separate on the larger instances.

The GA generally beats SA there. Its population retains several structurally
different partitions at once, and Order Crossover can recombine a good customer
grouping from one parent with a good ordering from another. SA explores a single
trajectory, so a fixed budget buys it less structural diversity, and its
advantages --- simplicity and low per-iteration cost --- matter less once the
Split DP dominates the cost of evaluating a move.

ALNS is stronger still on the larger instances, and for a structural reason. A
single swap or 2-opt move changes a solution locally; a destroy-and-repair step
removes a whole neighbourhood or an entire route and rebuilds it with look-ahead,
so one iteration can cross a barrier that would take a long, mostly-rejected
sequence of single moves. The regret-based repairs matter here: they place the
customer that would suffer most from waiting rather than the one that is cheapest
right now, which is exactly the myopia that traps greedy insertion. The adaptive
weights then concentrate effort on whichever destroy/repair pair is working on
this instance, so the method tunes itself rather than needing tuning.

\subsection{Why the Split decoder is the important component}

Both metaheuristics owe most of their quality to the Split DP of
section~\ref{sec:split} rather than to their own operators. Split converts any
permutation into the \emph{cheapest} feasible set of routes along that order, so
the search never wastes effort on repairing infeasible solutions or on choosing
route boundaries. The operators only have to explore orderings; the hard,
constrained part of the problem is solved exactly at every evaluation.

\section{Reproducing These Results}

The full pipeline is three commands from a clean checkout:

\begin{verbatim}
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python run_experiments.py       # writes results/ and the tables above
python generate_figures.py      # writes the figures above
\end{verbatim}

Every solver run is appended to a SQLite results store, one row per run tagged
with the git commit that produced it, and the tables above are generated from
that store rather than typed by hand. The figures read the same rows, so the
numbers and the plots cannot disagree.

Correctness rests on brute force wherever that is affordable. The Split decoder
is checked against exhaustive enumeration of every segmentation; Branch \& Bound
against exhaustive enumeration of every partition-into-ordered-routes; the lower
bound is asserted never to exceed the true optimum, since a bound that
overestimates would silently return a wrong answer labelled optimal; and the
feasibility checker is cross-examined by an independently written reference
implementation over thousands of random solutions. The notebook
\texttt{Van Der Linde\_Code.ipynb} is retained unchanged as the original
artefact, and a parity test pins the numbers it produced.
